Abdi Ali Barkad It is time to speak frankly. Many former Ex-Italian-Somali (South-Somalia) intellectuals, academics, and politicians appear to be preoccupied with the political affairs of the Republic of Somaliland, while conveniently overlooking the enormous challenges confronting their own country. They continue to knock on the wrong door, investing their intellectual energy and political resources in a matter that requires neither their permission nor their approval. Let us remind them of a fundamental political reality The people of Somaliland made their decision not to remain in the union with Southern Somalia . In 1991, Somaliland restored its independence following the collapse of the Somali Republic, which had been established in 1960. That political union came to an end, and Somaliland embarked on its own political journey. Whether some people accept this reality or not does not change the historical and political position of Somaliland. After 35 years, it is reasonable to ask the intellectuals and politicians of former Italian Somalia a fundamental question: For more than three decades, your country has struggled to establish effective national institutions, lasting political stability, and a functioning system of governance. The federal arrangement you adopted has not delivered the peace, unity, and institutional stability that the Somali people were promised. Political confrontations between Villa Somalia and Federal Member States continue. Armed conflicts persist in different parts of the country. National institutions remain fragile, and the security sector continues to face serious questions concerning its independence, inclusiveness, and national representation. There are also serious allegations concerning the mismanagement and disposal of public assets and the weakening of state institutions under successive administrations, particularly the current leadership. These are not minor political disagreements. They are fundamental questions about the survival, credibility, and future of your state. Now, compare this with Somaliland. Over the same period, Somaliland has developed its own political institutions, conducted six presidential elections, and elected four presidents through direct universal suffrage under a multiparty democratic system. This achievement deserves serious political and academic examination, regardless of one’s position on Somaliland’s international recognition. What is particularly difficult to understand is why intellectuals, academics, and experienced politicians continue to spend so much time debating Somaliland’s internal affairs while their own political house remains in such disarray. Where is that same intellectual energy when it comes to rebuilding national institutions? Where is the same political determination when federal authorities are in conflict with one another? Where is the same academic scrutiny when questions arise about public resources, national security, corruption, and the accountability of those governing your country? Why is Somaliland constantly on your political agenda when the most urgent national problems are at your own doorstep? An intellectual’s responsibility is to confront reality, not escape from it. A politician’s duty is to serve the people, not to distract them from the failures of governance. We respectfully but firmly advise you to redirect your attention towards the internal affairs of your own country. Concentrate on building a functioning federal system. Establish genuine national institutions. Create an inclusive and professional national army. Resolve political disputes between federal and regional authorities. Protect public assets. Fight corruption. Restore public confidence in government and give your people a reason to believe in their country’s future. These are the responsibilities that demand your experience, knowledge, and political leadership. Somaliland is not responsible for the political failures of your country, and its people should not be expected to put their political future on hold because others have failed to resolve their own problems. You cannot build a nation by constantly questioning the political choices of your neighbors. You cannot establish credible leadership while ignoring failures within your own administration. And you cannot lecture others about statehood when your own state-building project remains unfinished. My message is neither an invitation to hostility nor a rejection of dialogue. It is a call for political maturity, intellectual honesty, and respect for the choices of peoples. Respect Somaliland’s political journey. Accept that its people have their own political aspirations and priorities. Stop treating Somaliland as a permanent subject of political obsession. You have a country that needs your attention, a population that needs effective leadership, institutions that need rebuilding, and a political system that urgently needs reform. Put your own house in order. Rebuild your nation. Resolve your internal divisions. Establish credible institutions. And when you have made meaningful progress in those responsibilities, we can sit down and discuss matters of mutual interest as neighbours. Until then, stop knocking on Somaliland’s door. Your own house is the one that needs urgent attention. Respect political realities. Respect the people’s choices. Build your own nation first. somalia.title: Somali and Turkish Police Chiefs Meet as Haramcad Partnership Continues - FTL Somalia
somalia.summary: Somali Police Commissioner Brigadier General Asad Osman Abdullahi recently met with General Hüseyin Ediz Tercanoğlu, the Commander of the Turkish Police Special Operations Department, in Türkiye to enhance security cooperation. Their discussions focused on improving the operational capabilities of the Somali Police Force, particularly the Haramcad special police unit, which has received extensive training and equipment from Turkey. This partnership aims to strengthen Somalia's security framework amid ongoing political tensions in Mogadishu. Critics argue that Turkey's support may be too closely aligned with President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's administration, raising concerns about potential political bias and civilian harm during operations. The effectiveness of the Haramcad unit, while improved through training, is contingent upon its integration within a broader security architecture that includes accountability mechanisms. As the partnership continues, the challenge remains to ensure that the unit serves the public interest rather than merely the political agenda of the current government.

Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia’s Election Crisis Deepens as Talks Collapse Posted by: Hanad Askar Opposition boycott threatens to undermine President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s proposed national consultations as political divisions deepen over elections, constitutional legitimacy and the future of Somalia’s democratic transition. 14 November, 2026 Share Tweet Somalia’s planned National Consultative Forum, announced by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud for November 14–18, has been postponed after political leaders failed to agree on the conditions and procedures governing the proposed talks, according to local media reports. The postponement represents another setback for efforts to resolve Somalia’s escalating political crisis, with opposition groups questioning the legitimacy of the government’s electoral roadmap and accusing Villa Somalia of attempting to dictate the terms of a dialogue whose outcome could determine the country’s political future. At the centre of the dispute is a fundamental disagreement over elections, the government’s mandate and the proposed extension of the current political arrangements. Opposition leaders have demanded internationally mediated negotiations and guarantees that electoral preparations will be suspended until a political agreement is reached. The government, however, has continued pursuing its electoral timetable, setting parliamentary elections for April 15, 2027, and a presidential vote for May 15, 2027. The controversy has intensified following a Supreme Court ruling concerning the expiration of the government’s mandate, raising further questions about the constitutional and political basis for continuing with its current arrangements. The precise legal implications of that ruling remain central to the dispute. A dialogue undermined by political mistrust The postponement was hardly unexpected. When President Mohamud announced the forum in late October, the government was already facing mounting pressure from opposition groups that had repeatedly challenged its approach to the electoral process. The Somali Future Council, one of the principal opposition groupings, had made clear that it would not participate without independent international mediation. Meanwhile, Nabad iyo Nolol, the political movement associated with former President Mohamed Abdullahi Farmaajo, maintained its distance from the broader opposition coalition, despite continuing contacts with Villa Somalia. The government’s decision to convene the forum without first securing agreement on its framework exposed a fundamental weakness in its approach: announcing political dialogue is not the same as building the consensus necessary to make it credible. Rather than resolving the disagreements that have paralysed Somalia’s political process, the proposed meeting appeared at risk of becoming another exercise in political positioning. International involvement fails to bridge the divide One significant development since the invitation was issued has been the changing diplomatic context. The United States, Britain, Türkiye and the European Union, collectively referred to as the Quartet, agreed to facilitate the proposed talks. Their involvement appeared to address at least part of the opposition’s demand for international engagement. However, the arrangement has failed to secure the participation of the Somali Future Council. The opposition grouping has maintained that international facilitation alone is insufficient and has insisted on formal international mediation. It has also informed the Quartet that it will not attend a meeting held at Villa Somalia, arguing that the proposed venue raises questions about the neutrality and ownership of the process. The National Unity Coalition, led by former Prime Minister Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke, and Nabad iyo Nolol have reportedly agreed in principle to accept the invitation. However, uncertainty remains over the location and final arrangements for the talks. The result is an increasingly fragmented political process in which the government risks proceeding without one of the country’s most significant opposition alliances. The conditions that were never met The opposition’s demands have remained broadly consistent. The Somali Future Council has called for the immediate suspension of election-related activities and the appointment of an independent and credible mediator. It has also proposed an alternative Transitional Direct Elections Model, combining direct voting with Somalia’s established 4.5 clan-based power-sharing formula. The proposal reflects opposition concerns that the government’s one-person, one-vote framework may be difficult to implement under the country’s current security, institutional and political conditions. The government has rejected the opposition’s preconditions and continued with preparations under the electoral commission’s timetable. It has also invited political rivals to participate in a forum whose agenda and organisational arrangements were largely determined by Villa Somalia, without first reaching agreement on the fundamental issues dividing the parties. This approach has reinforced opposition suspicions that the proposed dialogue is intended to secure political endorsement for decisions already taken by the government rather than negotiate a genuinely inclusive electoral settlement. The government’s insistence on moving forward while key political actors dispute the legitimacy of the process risks deepening the crisis it claims to be addressing. Farmaajo’s position complicates the opposition landscape Nabad iyo Nolol’s position has added another layer of uncertainty. The party has denied participating in joint opposition meetings, although it confirmed that military commanders visited former President Mohamed Abdullahi Farmaajo at his residence to deliver President Mohamud’s invitation. Farmaajo reportedly outlined conditions for dialogue, including a demand that negotiations resume from where they broke down in September and that the role of the international community be respected. The episode highlights the fragmented nature of Somalia’s opposition, where competing political calculations have made it difficult to establish a unified position against the government’s electoral plans. Nevertheless, the absence of agreement among opposition groups does not remove the government’s responsibility to establish a credible, constitutional and inclusive electoral process. Somalia faces a deeper political legitimacy crisis The postponement of the National Consultative Forum is about more than disagreements over meeting arrangements or diplomatic mediation. It reflects a much deeper crisis of political trust. Somalia’s electoral disputes have repeatedly exposed the fragility of its political institutions and the difficulty of reaching consensus on the transfer of power. The latest impasse risks reviving the very political confrontations that previous negotiations were intended to prevent. For President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s administration, the challenge is increasingly one of political legitimacy. A government cannot resolve a national electoral dispute simply by announcing a timetable, inviting selected political actors to a meeting or securing the participation of international partners. It must demonstrate that the process is constitutionally grounded, politically inclusive and accepted by the country’s principal stakeholders. With the proposed parliamentary and presidential elections scheduled for 2027, the consequences of continued deadlock could be considerable. Without a negotiated settlement, Somalia risks entering another period of institutional uncertainty, with competing claims over electoral authority and the legitimacy of the country’s political leadership. The immediate question is no longer simply when the National Consultative Forum will take place. It is whether President Mohamud’s government is prepared to negotiate the fundamental terms of the electoral process, or whether it intends to press ahead with its own roadmap despite the objections of major political opponents. Until that question is answered, another postponed meeting is unlikely to bring Somalia closer to the political consensus it urgently needs. Opposition groups are boycotting the talks, questioning the legitimacy of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's electoral roadmap and demanding internationally mediated negotiations. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia India, Somalia discuss strengthening defence cooperation, focus on maritime security and counter-terrorism Posted by: Horseed Staff India and Somalia have discussed ways to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation, with particular emphasis on maritime security, counter-terrorism and capacity building, during a high-level meeting in Mogadishu. 14 November, 2026 Share Tweet The discussions took place on Saturday between India’s External Affairs Ministry Secretary Sripriya Ranganathan and Somali Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi. The two officials also exchanged views on the evolving regional security environment, according to India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed the meeting in a post on social media platform X, saying the discussions focused on strengthening defence ties between the two countries. Secretary(CPV&OIA) @ranganathan_sr called on H.E Ahmed Moallim Fiqi, Defence Minister of Somalia. Discussions pertained to strengthening bilateral defence cooperation, particularly in the fields of maritime security, counter-terrorism and capacity building. They also shared views… pic.twitter.com/n7aFP2lr4K — Randhir Jaiswal (@MEAIndia) November 14, 2026 Ranganathan, who serves as Secretary for Consular, Passport, Visa and Overseas Indian Affairs, met Fiqi as part of her official visit to Somalia. First high-level Indian visit in recent years Ranganathan arrived in Mogadishu on Saturday for official engagements with Somalia’s leadership, marking the first high-level bilateral visit from India to the country in recent years. The High Commission of India in Nairobi, which is concurrently accredited to Somalia, said the visit would build on the “longstanding and friendly ties between the two countries”. During her stay, Ranganathan is scheduled to meet senior Somali officials to review existing bilateral cooperation and explore new areas of partnership in diplomatic, consular and developmental affairs. The visit comes as both countries seek to strengthen their engagement across several areas, including security and institutional capacity building. India and Somalia share longstanding ties India and Somalia have longstanding maritime and commercial connections dating back centuries. Formal diplomatic relations between the two countries were established in 1960, following Somalia’s independence. India closed its resident diplomatic mission in Mogadishu in 1991 after the outbreak of civil war. However, New Delhi has continued its engagement with Somalia through development assistance, capacity-building programmes and maritime security cooperation. India launches oral history initiative in Kenya Separately, the High Commission of India in Nairobi launched an oral history podcast series on Thursday titled The Bharat Connection: Living Memories, Shared History . The initiative aims to document the experiences and journeys of prominent members of the Indian-origin community in Kenya, highlighting the historical and cultural connections between the two countries. Indian High Commissioner to Kenya Adarsh Swaika said the project would capture personal stories reflecting the shared history and longstanding relationship between India and Kenya. Ranganathan's agenda includes meetings with senior Somali officials to review existing cooperation and explore new partnership opportunities in various sectors, reinforcing the commitment to enhance collaboration between the two nations.

football.summary: أعلنت لجنة الاستئناف بالاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم قرارًا مفاجئًا بشأن لقب الدوري السوداني، حيث ألغت قرارها السابق الذي منح اللقب لنادي المريخ، وأعادت اللقب لنادي الهلال. جاء هذا القرار بعد قبول طلب المراجعة المقدم من الهلال، الذي أكد استحقاقه للقب بعد فوزه على المريخ في المباراة الأخيرة من الموسم الماضي. وأوضحت اللجنة أنها عقدت اجتماعين في 9 و10 نوفمبر، حيث استندت إلى تقرير الحكم في المباراة. وأصدر نادي الهلال بيانًا رسميًا يعلن فيه استرداده للقب، مؤكدًا مكانته كأكثر الأندية تتويجًا بالبطولات في السودان. يذكر أن الموسم الماضي شهد جدلًا كبيرًا حول قانونية مشاركة بعض لاعبي الهلال، مما أدى إلى منح اللقب للمريخ بعد استئناف. هذا القرار يعيد الأمور إلى نصابها ويؤكد تفوق الهلال في الساحة الرياضية السودانية.
